canonicalExplanation.summary: A **function template** is a **blueprint**: `template <typename T> T larger(T a, T b)`. At **compile time**, each call with new argument types makes the compiler **instantiate** a separate, fully typed function: `larger<int>`, `larger<std::string>`. Nothing is checked or chosen at run time. The template only works for types that support **every operation it uses**, here `<`. In C++20 you can **state** that requirement with a concept (`std::totally_ordered<T>`) so a bad call fails clearly at the call site. If the two arguments deduce different types (`larger(3, 2.5)`), deduction fails: convert one or specify `larger<double>(3, 2.5)`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes separate largest functions for int, double and std::string, all identical except for the type. Then they write one template and call it with a struct that has no `<`, getting a wall of errors from inside the template. A constrained maximum template accepts two values with a valid ordering and common return behavior rather than assuming every type supports operator<. In this lesson you'll implement and instantiate a type-safe generic function for multiple value types.

examples.title: One larger() for ints, doubles and strings
examples.situation: A constrained maximum template accepts two values with a valid ordering and common return behavior rather than assuming every type supports operator<.
walkthrough: **A constrained maximum template:** template <std::totally_ordered T> larger(const T&, const T&).
**Accepts two values with a valid ordering and common return behavior:** int, double and std::string all work and return their own type.
**Rather than assuming every type supports operator<:** larger(Point{}, Point{}) will fail at the call with a clear constraint message.
examples.result: One function replaces three copies, and misuse is reported clearly.

examples.title: The copy-paste trio
examples.situation: Three largest functions differ only in type; a bug fix is applied to the int version and forgotten in the others.
walkthrough: Replace all three with one template.
Fixes now apply to every instantiation.
Tests call it with each type.
examples.result: One implementation, one fix, every type covered.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A function template is one runtime function that inspects an argument's dynamic type.
misconceptions.correction: The compiler instantiates a separate function for each set of template arguments at compile time. There's no run-time type inspection.

analogy.example: A function template is like **a cookie cutter**: one shape, pressed into different doughs (types) to make separate cookies (instantiations). It works only with doughs that hold a shape (support <); a concept is **the label "firm dough only"** printed on the cutter.
limitations: Cookie cutters work at bake time; templates work at compile time.
Mixing two doughs in one press (int and double) doesn't work.

steps.explanation: The constrained template accepts two values with a valid ordering.
It gives common return behavior for each type separately.
It does not assume every type supports operator<.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing template instantiation. Step 1, Instantiate int: T is int; result is 7. The constrained template accepts two values with a valid ordering. Step 2, Instantiate string: T is std::string; result is pear. It gives common return behavior for each type separately. Step 3, Reject: T is Point; error is constraint not satisfied. It does not assume every type supports operator<.

nearTransfer.prompt: Write template <typename T> void swap_values(T& a, T& b) and test it with int, std::string and std::vector<int>. Then write a constrained clamp_to(value, low, high) using std::totally_ordered.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a template sum_all(const std::vector<T>&) that returns T, constrained so T supports + and default construction (write your own concept or requires clause). Test with int, double and std::string, and read the error for a type without +.
scaffold: requires (T a, T b) { a + b; }.
expectedEvidence: Clear error for an unsupported type.

remediation.explanation: For each template list **every operation it uses on T**. Then either constrain T to those operations or document them, and test with every intended type.

recap.summary: To implement type-safe generic functions, write a function template once, let the compiler instantiate a typed version for each argument type at compile time, constrain the template to the operations it uses (for example with std::totally_ordered), and resolve deduction conflicts with explicit template arguments or conversions.
